"Bro, scene set hai? Canteen at one, full vibe," Preeti said, dropping her bag on the bench.
Pradeep grinned. "Set. But mujhe first ye batao, kal ka match dekha? Total paisa vasool."
"Dekha! That last over, arre, pure heart attack."
Their new classmate Jaya, sitting alone, frowned. "Paisa vasool... is there an English for it?"
Preeti stopped. "Honestly? No. That's why we say it in Hindi. 'Value for money' is too flat."
"And 'timepass'?"
"Same thing. English can't do it."
Jaya laughed. "Okay, I want to learn these. Teach me?"
"Deal," said Pradeep. "Lesson one: 'jugaad'."

qa.a: Preeti told Pradeep to meet at the canteen at one.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when Jaya asked whether there is an English word for "paisa vasool"?
qa.a: Preeti felt thoughtful and a little proud. Stopping to say that English is too flat for it shows that the mix is a real way to say things one language alone cannot.

qa.q: What did Pradeep and Preeti do after Jaya asked about the words, and why did it help?
qa.a: They offered to teach Jaya the words, starting with "jugaad". That turned the mixed talk from a private code into something Jaya could join.

qa.a: Jaya might feel a little left out, sitting alone and frowning at the words. Asking and being invited to learn them made Jaya feel included.

I am Shankar. My school in Vidarbha taught in Marathi and I learnt English from books. In Class 9 in the city school I read aloud once, and a boy imitated the way I said "world". Half the room laughed.
After that I kept my hand down. Even when I knew the answer I felt my throat tighten, and my face got hot. Teachers marked me "quiet".
Then Simran, who sat next to me, said one day, "I also stumble on 'thorough'. Want to make a reading pair? Ten minutes at lunch." We read paragraph after paragraph. By December I put my hand up, shaking a little, and the room was quiet in the good way.

qa.a: Shankar's school in Vidarbha taught in Marathi.

qa.a: Shankar felt ashamed and afraid of being laughed at again. The tight throat and hot face show it, and that is why the hand stayed down.

Every Sunday at four, my grandfather Omkar tells me about the day the river flooded his village. I'm Deepak, and I've heard it maybe thirty times: the boat, the tin trunk, his mother carrying the brass lamp. When I was fifteen I would say, "Nana, I know."
